nameStory: The name 'lantana' comes from the Latin name for the viburnum shrub, which has similar clusters of small flowers. Early botanists thought the flower clusters looked so much like viburnum that they borrowed the name, even though these plants aren't related at all!
description: Common lantana is a tropical shrub with dense, rounded clusters of tiny tubular flowers that come in bright colors like yellow, orange, red, or pink - often with multiple colors in the same cluster. This warm-weather plant grows 3-6 feet tall and wide with a bushy, spreading habit. While it's popular in gardens for its non-stop blooms and butterfly-attracting flowers, it's extremely rare in New England since it can't survive our winters outdoors.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny tubular flowers, each cluster about 2 inches across. Colors range from yellow and orange to red and pink, often changing color as they age - you might see yellow flowers turning orange or red in the same cluster. The flowers have a light, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, oval-shaped leaves with deeply toothed edges and a rough, sandpapery texture that feels scratchy when you rub them. The leaves have prominent veins and give off a strong, somewhat unpleasant smell when crushed - some people describe it as musty or pungent.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round berries that start green and turn dark blue or black when ripe, each about the size of a peppercorn. The berries are clustered together where the flowers used to be and are toxic to humans and pets.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, bushy shrub with square-ish stems that spread wider than they are tall. Branches tend to arch outward, creating a mounded appearance that can become quite sprawling if left unpruned.

habitat: In New England, common lantana is only found as a cultivated annual in gardens, containers, or as a houseplant, since it cannot survive freezing temperatures. You might spot it in summer flower beds, hanging baskets at garden centers, or in butterfly gardens where it's grown for its nectar-rich blooms.

seasonality.spring: Not visible outdoors in New England - any lantana plants are still indoors or not yet planted until after the last frost date.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and blooming season if grown as an annual. Flowers appear continuously from early summer through the first frost, with the most vibrant flower clusters appearing during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until the first hard frost kills the plant. Berries may develop and ripen to dark blue-black in late summer and early fall if flowers aren't deadheaded.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - any outdoor plants will be killed by frost. Only survives as a houseplant in heated indoor spaces.

funFact: Lantana flowers are like tiny mood rings - they actually change color as they age! A single flower cluster might start with yellow blooms that turn orange, then red, creating a beautiful rainbow effect that helps butterflies know which flowers have the most nectar (hint: it's usually the newest, youngest-colored ones).
confusionNotes: The dense flower clusters might remind you of viburnum or elderberry, but lantana's tropical appearance, rough-textured leaves, and square stems set it apart. Unlike those native shrubs, lantana has that distinctive scratchy leaf feel and strong smell when crushed.
contextualKnowledge: While lantana is beloved by gardeners for its continuous blooms and butterfly appeal, it's important to know that all parts of the plant are toxic to humans, pets, and livestock. In its native tropical range and other warm climates, it's considered one of the world's most invasive weeds, but New England's cold winters keep it in check.
compareHints: Common lantana is the only Lantana species you're likely to encounter in New England gardens. Among plants in the verbena family, it's easily distinguished by its woody shrub growth habit and clustered flowers - most other verbenas in our region are herbaceous plants with flowers arranged in spikes rather than dense, flat-topped clusters.
